The simple solution is to not view it as an interrupted action. Don't assume that the card needs to be in the trash to be considered destroyed. Moving to the trash is the end result of a card being tagged for destruction. 

We can go back and reference the rule for resolving triggers, that with consecutive triggers, the newest one is always resolved first. Being tagged for destruction is the first effect, which then triggers the destruction effect (so now resolve that first), then carry out the rest of destruction (move to trash). 

Everythibg here is very consistent with all current ruling on triggered effects. Sounds resolved to me.

Edit: I guess it is kinda interrupted, but that doesn't change how you resolve interrupted actions. Also Pydro, I agree that the wording of "when this card would be destroyed" could make it clearer, but it wouldn't trigger simultaneously with other "when a card is destroyed" triggers. Whether or not that is important is questionable, but relevant.

Consider the ramifications of one of the easiest villains in the game. Gloomy has out Pouch of Bones. If so, it would be nearly impossible to kill a cultist, if we applied this logic.

1) Cultist is called "destoryed" but still in play.

2) Gloomy's text triggers and brings out a zombie.

3) Pouch of Bones triggers and all targets heal H.

4) Cultist would leave play, but now has hp.

It could be right, but how or where were we supposed to figure it out. Nothing has ever been said anywhere about something like this. It might be possbile to base something on the new "can't be destroyed twice" rule, but this is the only thing we have ever heard about it, and there are some arguments against it.

Furthermore, if it wasn't for Sonic Mines and Explosive Wagons, everyone would get the rule wrong. There is no basis anywhere that these are different steps, and we have never heard of anything outside of these cards that it works this way. I am very happy with the following idea: destoryed = leaves play. The only excpetion to this is when a card needs to stay in play to resolve its own effect. However, all other triggers are still based on when it leaves play, not its destruction. So the order will be:

1) Card is called "destroyed."

The only problem is when this question came up, everyone said it is based on card order. So it would be:

2) Resolve any on destruction effect on a card in play before the original card, and all modifiers on the original card are still active.

3) Resolve the original card's on destruction effect with its modifiers.

4a) Original card leaves play and takes it modifiers.

5a). Resolve any on destruction effects on a card in play after the original card.

Or is it:

4b) Resolve any on destruction effects on a card in play after the original card, and all modifiers on the original card are still active.

5b) The original card finally leaves play.

Just for simoplicity's sake, I like the first explanation, where the original card's effect is always first. If the explanation is the second one, I am leaning towards "A," but if it really is that precise and involved, it deserves an official clarification. (Hence, my longer question above.)

posts.name: Pydro
posts.cooked:
Except, this is inconsistent with other rulings.

Consider the following "normal" situation:

1) Card is destroyed.

2) Card leaves play.

3) On destruction triggers.

First off, I think we can agree that in a normal situation the triggers won't happen between steps #2 and #3. If they do, I want a ruling saying this.

Now, there are 2 ways to interpret this situation.

A) destroyed = leaves play. This means, that when a card says "when X is destroyed" it can be read as "when X is destoryed and leaves play."

B) destroyed =/= leaves play. If so, then when a card says "when this card is destroyed" it doesn't really mean "is destoryed" what is really means is "when this card leaves play." Otherwise, it would inherently trigger between steps #1 and #2.

Now let's consider a card that has a self-destruct effect. We know that this is a special exemption, where a card is destroyed but has to stay in play until its text is resolved. So let's look at each of the above and see what would happen.

A) Since destroyed = leaves play, all other triggers won;t happen until the card left play, but we know this special ruling that the self-destruct effect has to happen before it leaves play. Therefore, the self-destruct always happens first.

B) Since destroyed =/= leaves play, it has to mean "leaves play" otherwise the normal conditions don't work. If so, it would only trigger in this case after it leaves play, once again triggering the self-destruct first.

dypaca:

That implicit text would cause Explosive Wagon to behave the way it has been ruled, and is one of the possible timing scenarios that was being argued for (I think by Foote).

Yes that is my stance.

I think we have to look at the spirit of the Wagon/Mine ruling. What primary idea is it trying to accomplish? Both were off cuff rulings, so I would rather view them generally. Both rulings are really trying to address a core issue of the SotM game system in my estimation, that being the elimination of sourceless effects, especially sourceless damage. That is the heart of it. By absolute nessesity of the game system, Wagon/Mines can not resolve their damage effect if they are not in play to do so. Why do you think it is possible to interupt normal damage sequences like Omnitrons Electropulse? Because by removing that card from play it is no longer able to continue the resolution of the effect.

It is also worth noting here that the 3rd off cuff ruling eliminated the idea that Wagon, once destroyed, can be destroyed a second time as a way to interupt its damage sequence. This is significant because it also eliminates the possibility of errata with wording of "when this card would be destroyed, instead do…". Because the intention is that Wagon is still considered "destroyed" and still in play. That errata's effect would kick in before the card was tagged as destroyed, opening back up the possibility that Wagon could be destroyed a second time to interupt the damage sequence. That is clearly not the intention.

The overwelming majority consensus before all of this was that cards are removed from play immediatly upon being destroyed. The rulebook definition seems to support that and there was never any issue taken with that interpretation. (Someone will bring up Solar Flare in response to this point. I get no general consenses is "safe", but there is little reason to question every major consensus. Even Christopher varied his initial Solar Flare ruling slightly to better fit with the forums general idea of how the card should function remember).

Because Wagon/Mine functions slightly differently due soley to a nessesity within the games mechanics, it does not follow that all cards would function the same way since there is not the same nessesity to do so. That interpretation, at this point with these rulings, is a fairly large logical stretch that has far wider implications to the game as a whole than at first glance. It is much more simple and sensible, given all of the above, that Wagon/Mines are a slight deviation from the norm due simply to the nature of their effect trigger instead of jumping to the "this changes everything!" conclusions. And if you also reach the same conclusion as myself after all of this, the question of when those effects actually trigger naturally falls upon the "resolve simultanious triggers by card order played" rule (and remove Wagon/Mines from play after they complete their damage sequence).

This is the more stable interpretation of those presented in this thread so far. I just do not see how I could accept any of the other interpretations as true at this point in time without specific clarification to the contrary.

Wouldn't an implicit rules trigger on all cards that read "When this card is destroyed, put it in the trash." solve all these issues?  This would mean when destruction triggers were involved, the destroyed card would be in play up until the point in the card order in which any of its own explicit destruction triggers resolved, and then it would go to the trash due to the implicit trigger.

I agree and I like the term of implicit vs explicit triggers. Excplicit triggers are ones that come right from card text. Implicit triggers are baked-in aspects of Core Game System terms. Those Core Terms are found in the glossary of the rulebook. 

For instance, One-Shots have an implicit trigger that states once the effect is over, it is moved to the trash. See the rulebook definition for One-Shots to see what I am talking about. Destroyed is also in that list of core game terms that have an implicit trigger. And that implicit trigger is word for word what you described.

We do not associate the timing of when a One-Shot leaves play with the timing of other explicit triggers. It just happens immediatly after the One-Shot has completed its task.  So why would Destruction be any different in this sense.

Another data point for this Explosive Wagon thing comes from observing behavior of the App (whose makers clearly spent a lot of time getting Christiopher Badell to clarify edge cases).  While they don't have EW implemented yet, the behavior of One-Shots may be illuminating.  When played, One-Shots go to the "Cards in Play" section of the board, and they stay there until every piece of their text has finished resolving.  Only then do they go to the Trash.  Characters who have chain-able "play a card" cards, such as Tachyon and Wraith will often have 2 or 3 One-Shots stacked up on their board, which all collapse into the Trash at once when the chain completes.

I would expect EW to similarly remain on the board while it was processing its own "destroyed" effect, and only go to the Trash when that was complete.

That's not a full answer to the "destroyed" issue, but it's a data point.
